opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and one I get quite a bit. I'd say the natural order is to start with *Build a Large Language Model from Scratch* and then move on to *Build a Reasoning Model from Scratch*. The first book is really about the foundations: how you go from raw text to tokens, how the attention mechanism works, how you put together a GPT-style architecture, pre-train it, and then fine-tune it, both for classification and for following instructions. It gives you that mental model of what's actually happening inside an LLM.

The reasoning book builds on top of that. It assumes you're comfortable with how an LLM generates text, and then it asks: how do we get these models to work through problems step by step? That includes inference-time scaling techniques, like spending more compute while generating, and then training methods such as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and distillation. Those ideas make a lot more sense if you already understand next-token prediction and the training loop.

That said, I tried to write the second book so it can stand on its own. Rather than having readers build everything again, it starts from an existing pre-trained open-weight model. So if you already have a solid background, say you've implemented a transformer before or you work with these models daily, you could go straight to the reasoning book and only look back at the first one when something feels unclear. But if you're newer to this, or you want the full picture from the ground up, I'd definitely read them in order. They're designed to complement each other, almost like volume one and volume two.

r001.rationale: The response says the reasoning book starts from an existing pretrained open-weight model and that experienced readers could go straight to it, so the first book is not a prerequisite.

r002.rationale: It recommends reading the books in order for newer readers or those wanting the full picture, and describes the first book’s pretraining and fine-tuning stages.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, and the short answer is that they're designed to be read in order, but you don't strictly have to.

The first book, Build a Large Language Model from Scratch, is really the foundation. You implement a GPT-style architecture from the ground up, in plain PyTorch, pre-train it on a small dataset, and then do the fine-tuning stages, classification fine-tuning and instruction fine-tuning. By the end of it you have a complete, working LLM that you understand at the level of every tensor operation. That's the mental model everything else builds on.

The reasoning book picks up right where that one leaves off. The premise is that you start with a pre-trained base model, and now the question becomes: how do you get it to reason? So we go through things like inference-time scaling, chain-of-thought style approaches, and then training-based methods like reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and distillation. And because the model you're working with is essentially the one from the first book, you're not wrestling with a huge unfamiliar codebase. The code stays small enough that you can hold it in your head.

That said, I did try to make the second book self-contained. If you already know how transformers work, you've trained models before, and you just want the reasoning part, you can jump straight in. I include enough of a recap of the architecture so you're not lost, and the pre-trained weights are provided, so you don't need to go through pre-training yourself.

So my recommendation is roughly this: if you're newer to LLMs, or you've only used them through APIs and never looked under the hood, start with the first book. It'll pay off. If you're a practitioner who's already comfortable with the internals and you're mainly curious about why reasoning models behave the way they do, you can start with the second one and go back to the first if you hit a spot where you want more depth.

And honestly, one thing I'd add is that these are meant to be worked through, not just read. The value comes from actually running the code, breaking it, and changing things. If you read them like a novel you'll get maybe thirty percent of what's there.

r001.rationale: The response says the reasoning book is self-contained, provides pretrained weights, and can be started directly by readers who already know transformer internals. This communicates that the first book is not a prerequisite.

r002.rationale: It describes the first book as covering pretraining and fine-tuning, says the reasoning book builds on it, and recommends that newer readers start with the first book before moving to the second.

astra-6.text:
I’d recommend starting with Build a Large Language Model from Scratch if you’re new to implementing language models. That gives you the foundation: how the architecture works, how you train it, and how you fine-tune it. Then Build a Reasoning Model from Scratch is a natural next step, focusing on how to develop reasoning capabilities on top of that foundation.

But if you already understand how LLMs work and you’re comfortable implementing them in PyTorch, you can jump straight into the reasoning book. It really depends on your starting point.
